query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multi-element solid-solution high-entropy superconductors outside Nb‐Ta and titanium‐rich regimes, an optimal degree of chemical disorder enhances superconductivity by strengthening electron-phonon coupling, whereas excessive disorder increases electron scattering and degrades the superconducting transition temperature (Tc).
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy solid solution containing at least five elements with each element present at no less than 5 atomic percent, prepared under conditions yielding moderate atomic ordering (annealed state).
generation.intervention: Thermal processing modification via rapid quenching to increase chemical disorder compared to the annealed (more ordered) sample.
generation.conditions: All samples maintain identical overall composition, phase purity, and measurement conditions; only the thermal processing (and hence the degree of chemical disorder) is varied.
generation.structural_mediator: The level of atomic-scale chemical disorder, which influences the local density of states at the Fermi level and thereby the electron scattering rate.
generation.mechanism: Moderate disorder may locally enhance electron-phonon coupling by creating beneficial bonding variations, but when disorder becomes too high it increases electron scattering, thereby reducing Cooper pair formation and lowering Tc.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the annealed, moderately ordered baseline, the rapidly quenched (more disordered) sample will exhibit a lower Tc and a broader superconducting transition, reflecting degraded pairing efficiency due to excessive scattering.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the annealed sample with moderate chemical order.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under the constraint that the alloy is a single-phase, solid-solution HEA containing at least five elements (each ≥5 atomic percent) and is measured under controlled low-temperature superconducting conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold at which disorder shifts from being beneficial to detrimental remains undefined and may vary with specific alloy compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of high-entropy alloy samples with identical compositions: one set is annealed to promote atomic ordering, while the other is rapidly quenched to enhance chemical disorder. Measure superconducting properties across both sets under identical low-temperature conditions.
measurements: Critical temperature (Tc) via resistivity and magnetic susceptibility measurements
Structural characterization (using X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy) to verify the degree of chemical disorder
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the quenched (more disordered) sample does not show a significant reduction in Tc or instead shows a sharper (narrower) superconducting transition than the annealed baseline sample.

cited_evidence.text: We study the effects of the chemical short-range order (SRO) on the thermal conductivity of the refractory high-entropy alloy HfNbTaTiZr using atomistic simulation. Samples with different degrees of chemical SRO are prepared by a Monte Carlo scheme. With increasing SRO, a tendency of forming HfTi and TiZr clusters is found. The phonon density of states is determined from the velocity auto-correlation function and chemical SRO modifies the high-frequency part of the phonon density of states. Lattice heat conductivity is calculated by non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations. The heat conductivity of the random alloy is lower than that of the segregated binary alloys. Phonon scattering by SRO precipitates might be expected to reduce scattering times and, therefore, decrease thermal conductivity. We find that, in contrast, due to the increase of the conductivity alongside SRO cluster percolation pathways, SRO increases the lattice heat conductivity by around 12 %. This is expected to be a general result, extending to other HEAs.

Polymorphism, which describes the occurrence of different lattice structures in a crystalline material, is a critical phenomenon in materials science and condensed matter physics. Recently, configuration disorder was compositionally engineered into single lattices, leading to the discovery of high-entropy alloys and high-entropy oxides. For these novel entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter with extremely high structural stability, is polymorphism still possible? Here by employing in situ high-pressure synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction, we reveal a polymorphic transition from face-centred-cubic ( fcc ) structure to hexagonal-close-packing ( hcp ) structure in the prototype CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy. The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures. As pressure is increased, the critical temperature for the hcp -to- fcc transformation also rises.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Among the various systems of alloying elements studied, the Ta 20 Nb 20 Hf 20 Zr 20 Ti 20 alloy seems to be attractive due to its reduced density of 9.94 g/cm 3 [ [2] , [3] ], few publications [ [4] , [5] , [6] ] deal with thr thermodynamic properties of certain compositions of the Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti.

frame.system: A solid-solution high-entropy alloy containing at least five elements (each at a minimum of 5 atomic percent) that falls outside the well‐studied Nb‐Ta and titanium‐rich systems.
frame.goal: To determine the mechanistic origin of superconductivity in these uncharacterized high-entropy alloys—specifically, how chemical disorder and multi-element mixing affect the density of states and electron pairing.
frame.limitation: Precedent studies have focused on Nb-Ta matrices and titanium-rich systems, so the controlling factors for superconductivity in other high-entropy alloy compositions remain unidentified.
root_cause_cues: do not establish what controls superconductivity
constraints: each element present at no less than 5 atomic percent
frame.regime: Low-temperature superconducting regime where T_c and transition sharpness are measured under controlled compositional and microstructural (order/disorder) conditions.
prior_attempts: Studies on Nb-Ta based high-entropy superconductors
Investigations on titanium-rich, heavy transition metal systems with partial ordering
frame.mechanistic_hypothesis: Superconductivity in these high-entropy alloys is predominantly governed by the degree of chemical disorder, which modulates electronic scattering and the density of states at the Fermi level. An optimal level of disorder enhances electron-phonon coupling and pairing, whereas excessive disorder increases pair-breaking scattering, leading to a suppressed critical temperature (T_c).
frame.controlled_comparison: Prepare two samples with identical overall compositions (meeting the five-element, 5% minimum criterion): one sample is annealed to promote atomic ordering (minimizing disorder) and a second sample is rapidly quenched to enhance chemical disorder. This comparison tests the effect of disorder on superconducting properties.
frame.predicted_observations: Relative to the baseline (annealed, more ordered sample), the quenched (more disordered) sample should exhibit a lower T_c and a broader superconducting transition if the hypothesis is correct, indicating that excessive scattering reduces the pairing efficiency.
frame.applicable_boundary_conditions: The test is valid when all other variables (e.g., composition, phase purity, and measurement conditions) are held constant, ensuring that the only significant difference is the degree of chemical order/disorder introduced by the thermal treatment.
frame.supporting_evidence: Previous work on disordered superconductors in binary and ternary alloys has shown that moderate disorder can initially enhance electron-phonon coupling up to a critical point, beyond which increased scattering degrades T_c. These observations support the idea that in complex, multi-element systems, disorder plays a pivotal role in electronic structure and superconducting behavior.
frame.falsification_outcome: If the quenched sample (with higher disorder) shows no significant difference in T_c or even exhibits enhanced superconducting properties compared to the annealed sample, then the hypothesis—that chemical disorder beyond an optimal threshold degrades superconductivity—would be falsified.

decision.trend: Early high‐entropy alloy research focused on tailoring mechanical strength, phase stability, and transport properties in systems dominated by Nb‐Ta and Ti‐rich compositions. Researchers used controlled processing (e.g., annealing, casting, and quenching) to modulate disorder or short‐range order and thereby influence properties such as thermal conductivity and deformation behavior. More recently, studies—such as those addressing chemical short‐range order (PMC11375216) and refractory Nb-based systems (PMC11206460)—have hinted that the degree of atomic disorder profoundly impacts electron scattering and related transport phenomena. Despite these advances, the precise link between chemical disorder and superconducting behavior in HEAs falling outside the well‐studied matrices remains uncharted.
decision.unsolved: The fundamental mechanism by which controlled chemical disorder modulates the density of states and electron pairing – and thus the superconducting transition temperature and sharpness – in multi‐element solid-solution HEAs (with ≥5 elements, each ≥5 at.%) outside the Nb‐Ta and titanium-rich regimes is still unresolved.
decision.lever: thermal processing (annealing to induce ordering versus rapid quenching to enhance disorder)
decision.why: This approach directly builds on the trend that controlled thermal treatments can adjust the degree of chemical disorder, which has been shown to affect key electronic scattering processes in related high‐entropy systems. By preparing otherwise identical samples with different disorder levels, the experiment will test the mechanistic hypothesis that an optimal disorder level maximizes electron-phonon coupling for superconductivity, while excessive disorder degrades T_c. The design leverages past findings on disorder-induced changes in transport properties and short-range order to address the outstanding question.
